claims.text: Yield strength in single-crystal FeNiCrMn is anomalously insensitive to strain rate during the elastic-to-plastic transition.
The onset of yielding is driven by thermal unlocking of Lomer-Cottrell locks through stacking-fault accumulation.
Phase transformation and classical dislocation-nucleation barriers are not the dominant causes of yielding.
The initial single-crystal FeNiCrMn alloy has an FCC structure.
The initial material contains pre-existing stacking-fault networks and Lomer-Cottrell locks formed during processing or initial loading.
Removing grain boundaries isolates intrinsic deformation mechanisms.
Lomer-Cottrell locks and stacking-fault networks impede dislocation motion and are the primary barrier to yielding.
At low temperatures, Lomer-Cottrell locks are stable and require high stress to unlock.
Increasing temperature or accumulated strain thermally facilitates lock unlocking through stacking-fault accumulation.
Deformation shifts from TWIP to TRIP or simple slip as temperature or strain increases.
Lock unlocking decouples yield strength from the strain-rate sensitivity associated with dislocation-nucleation rates.
Yield strength will vary minimally with strain rate from 77 K to 600 K.
The HCP-phase fraction, if TRIP occurs, will correlate more strongly with temperature than with strain rate.
The density of unlocked dislocations will correlate more strongly with temperature than with strain rate.
Yield strength at 600 K will be lower than at 77 K.
Traditional FCC metals such as Ag and Cu are highly strain-rate sensitive because of thermally activated dislocation nucleation and glide.
Lomer-Cottrell locks are less prevalent or less stable in traditional FCC metals than in the proposed HEA.
The mechanism may not apply to polycrystals dominated by grain-boundary sliding or precipitation hardening, or to alloys whose stacking-fault energy prevents lock formation.
The cited evidence concerns CoNiCrFeMn nanowires simulated at a fixed strain rate of 10^8 s^-1 rather than bulk FeNiCrMn single crystals tested over variable low strain rates.
Detection of an FCC-to-BCC transformation as the primary deformation mode at yield would falsify the proposed lock-unlocking mechanism.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis excludes phase transformation as the driver, but the mechanism invokes a shift to TRIP and the predicted outcome proposes HCP-phase fraction as a key correlate. The distinction between a secondary transformation and a transformation-driven yielding mechanism is not made explicit.
